statement: The CCSMAF/CFSC is an introductory safety course intended for all new firearm users.
People who want to acquire restricted firearms must also pass the restricted firearms safety course (CRFSC) exams.
The Canadian Firearms Program is managed by the RCMP in cooperation with provincial Chief Firearms Officers.
The Canadian Firearms Program's activities include licensing, delivering the safety course, public education and import/export controls.
CFSC instructors and examiners must be recognized by the Chief Firearms Officer of the province or territory where the course is taken.
Every firearm accident involves breaking at least one of the vital safety rules.
Vital rule 1 (T/A): treat every firearm as if it were loaded.
Vital rule: always point the firearm in the safest direction and never at yourself or anyone else.
Vital rule: keep your finger off the trigger and outside the trigger guard except when firing.
A firearm should only be handed over or received when its action is open and it is unloaded.
The fourth vital rule requires opening the action and PROVING the firearm is safe (chamber and magazine empty) before handling it.
The first step of PROVE is to point the firearm in the safest direction.
PROVE sequence: point safe, remove cartridges, open action and check chambers, verify feeding path, examine bore.
The last PROVE step is examining the bore, with a rod or visually, to make sure it is not obstructed.
A proven firearm remains safe only while the person who proved it keeps direct control of it.
Licence holders must notify the Canadian Firearms Program of a change of address within 30 days.
A possession-only licence (POL) allows borrowing firearms of the authorized class, while a PAL also allows buying, inheriting or otherwise acquiring them.
Provincial/territorial laws may require blaze orange, restrict shooting near roads or dwellings and limit motor-vehicle use; municipalities may ban discharge entirely.
Pointing a firearm, loaded or unloaded, at another person without lawful excuse is a Criminal Code offence (indictable: up to 5 years).
Storing, displaying, transporting or handling firearms contrary to the regulations carries up to 2 years (first offence) or 5 years (subsequent) on indictment.
Good practices: keep an inventory of your firearms with photos and manuals in a safe place, and avoid advertising that you own firearms.
In a firearm, burning powder produces expanding gases that push the projectile out of the barrel.
The matchlock was unusable in rain or strong wind because the burning match could go out.
The flintlock produced a spark by friction of flint on the steel battery and was the most reliable early ignition system.
The percussion lock used a small metal cap containing a shock-sensitive explosive.
Early breech-loaders failed because expanding gases leaked through gaps between breech parts.
In a modern cartridge, the firing pin strikes the primer, which ignites the propellant; the case expands to seal the breech.
Cartridges are easy to load, prevent gas leaks, are generally weatherproof and more reliable, which made repeating firearms possible.
A shotshell contains shot, powder and primer in a case, with a wad separating the powder from the projectiles.
FFFFg (priming powder) is the finest black powder, used only for priming flintlock pans and never as a propellant charge.
Black powder grades: Fg is coarsest; FFFg is the most common, used in almost all muzzleloading revolvers and pistols.
Black powder is classed as an explosive and ignites easily from heat, friction, static electricity or sudden shock.
Old muzzleloaders must be inspected by a competent gunsmith before being fired.
To make sure a muzzleloader is not primed: point safely, check the hammer is not cocked, check for a cap or priming powder, and remove it.
A ramrod marked at the empty-bore depth shows whether a muzzleloader barrel is loaded.
Always pour powder into a muzzleloader with a volumetric measure, never directly from the container, flask or horn.
Under safe storage rules, a muzzleloader is considered loaded when there is powder and/or a projectile in the barrel.
Never use black powder in a modern cartridge firearm not designed for it, and never substitute smokeless powder for black powder.
Black powder is corrosive and attracts moisture; clean after every session, since carbon buildup can leave glowing embers that ignite a new charge.
Treat a muzzleloader misfire as a hangfire: keep it pointed in a safe direction and wait at least 60 seconds.
After the first shot from a multi-barrel muzzleloader, check the projectile position in the other barrel since recoil may have moved it forward.
A loaded muzzleloader may be transported between hunting sites only with the cap or flint removed; never store it with powder inside.
The three main parts of a modern firearm are the barrel, the action and the stock.
The front end of the barrel is the muzzle, the rear end is the chamber, and the calibre is often stamped on the barrel.
The action holds the parts that load, fire, and extract and eject cartridges or cases.
Keep the safety on while loading and take it off only when ready to fire, but never rely on it: a loaded firearm with the safety on can still fire.
A clip-type magazine (chargeur) is removable while a magasin is fixed; both hold a reserve of cartridges in repeating firearms.
Firing sequence: trigger releases firing pin, which strikes primer; primer flame ignites powder; gases push projectile out.
The three classes of firearms are non-restricted, restricted and prohibited; prohibited are the most controlled.
Many air guns are regulated by the Firearms Act because of their high velocity, so all air guns must be handled with ACTS and PROVE.
Almost all firearm accidents can be prevented by following basic safety rules, chiefly the vital four ACTS and PROVE.
Firearms should be stored unloaded, with ammunition kept separately and locked up, out of sight and out of reach of children.
Keeping firearms and ammunition out of sight during storage and transport reduces theft and unauthorized use.
At a range, load only when at the firing line and ready to shoot, and unload before leaving it.
Never cross a fence, ditch or obstacle, climb or run with a loaded firearm, and never throw a firearm across an obstacle.
Never lean a loaded firearm against a vehicle, tree or wall: it can fall and discharge.
Only carry unloaded firearms in a car or boat; many accidents happen when firearms are put in or taken out of vehicles.
Before loading, check the bore for obstructions and use only the correct ammunition for the firearm, carrying only that type.
Positively identify the target before shooting; never shoot at movement, colour, shape or sound.
A riflescope is not binoculars and must never be used to identify people, animals or objects.
Do not shoot if the projectile may hit a hard surface or water, at targets near buildings, or at targets on a hilltop.
Secure locking devices (trigger locks, cable/chain locks) block the action, must be properly installed, and are not compatible with every firearm.
You should carry only ammunition designed for the firearm you are using and the type of shooting planned.
In a rifled barrel, the metal ridges between the grooves are called lands.
Rifling makes the bullet spin as it leaves the barrel, giving it stability in flight.
Calibre is the bore diameter of a rifled firearm, given in thousandths of an inch or in millimetres.
The terms rimfire and centrefire describe where the primer is located on the cartridge head and where the firing pin strikes.
The most important point is that the designation on the cartridge head matches the data stamped on the barrel.
If a firearm has no stamp, take it to a qualified person who can measure the chamber and advise on ammunition.
A firearm's stamp may be missing or wrong if the firearm was modified, so it should be checked by a qualified person.
Improperly reloaded ammunition can cause malfunctions or make the firearm explode; never use reloads unless sure they were made correctly.
A rifle cartridge has four basic components: bullet, propellant powder, case and primer.
Hunting bullets are often soft-point or hollow-point, designed to expand on impact so most energy goes into the target.
The primer contains a chemical mixture that explodes when struck by the firing pin, igniting the propellant.
In rimfire ammunition, the priming compound is inside the rim; the firing pin crushes the soft rim to fire it.
All rimfire cartridges are .22 or .17HMR calibre.
.22 Magnum cartridges are not interchangeable with other .22 cartridges.
Dry-firing (firing with no cartridge in the chamber) a rimfire firearm can damage it.
Centrefire ammunition, used in more powerful firearms, has its primer in the centre of the case head.
Cartridges with different designations are not interchangeable even if they share a calibre (e.g., .303 Savage and .303 British).
The headstamp on a cartridge gives the cartridge name, calibre, manufacturer and whether it is regular or magnum.
Reading the cartridge headstamp is the only way to make sure the cartridge matches the firearm.
A rifled shotgun barrel spins slugs or sabots, making them like rifle bullets with greater accuracy and range.
Shotgun gauge is the number of lead balls of bore diameter that together weigh one pound.
The .410 is the only shotgun calibre that states the actual bore diameter (0.410 inch).
Choke is the narrowing of a shotgun bore toward the muzzle; it controls the spread of the shot.
Full choke gives the narrowest pattern; modified, improved and cylinder give progressively wider patterns.
A cylinder bore has no choke and is often used for larger shot such as buckshot or for rifled slugs.
A shotgun shell has five components; the wad separates the propellant from the shot, seals the gases and protects the shot.
Using steel shot in some shotgun barrels can damage the firearm; check the manufacturer's manual or a gunsmith.
Shell lengths marked on boxes and chambers (e.g., 70, 76, 89 mm for 12 gauge) are the length after firing.
Measuring an unfired shell is misleading: a 3-inch shell may measure only 2 3/4 in before firing, which could cause an accident.
Firing shells longer than the barrel stamp indicates can burst the barrel.
Some European shotguns have 2 and 2 1/2-inch chambers; firing 2 3/4-inch shells in them is dangerous.
A 20-gauge shell can slip into a 12-gauge chamber and lodge in the forcing cone; firing a 12-gauge shell behind it can burst the barrel.
Be sure of your target and what is beyond it; if a shot may be unsafe, do not shoot.
Factors affecting trajectory include gravity, air resistance, initial velocity and mass.
The muzzle must be raised above horizontal to compensate for gravity; the projectile crosses the line of sight twice.
A misfire is a cartridge that fails to fire; such cartridges must not be reused and must be disposed of properly.
A hangfire is a delay in ignition after the firing pin strikes the primer.
In a hangfire, removing the cartridge too quickly can let it fire outside the chamber and burst the case, causing injury.
A squib load has no powder; the primer may push the bullet into the barrel where it lodges, and firing another shot can burst the barrel.
If the trigger is pulled and nothing fires, wait 60 seconds with the muzzle in a safe direction, then open the action, remove the ammunition, PROVE safe and check for bore obstruction.
You may keep a reasonable quantity of sporting ammunition for personal use, not for resale (Natural Resources Canada).
Ammunition for non-restricted firearms must not be stored near the firearm unless stored in a securely locked container or compartment that cannot easily be broken into.
Ammunition must never be displayed with a firearm.
Store ammunition in a cool, dry place, preferably in a ventilated container; an unvented container can create an explosion hazard in a fire.
The safest way to transport ammunition is in its original container.
Never use smokeless powder in place of black powder or vice versa.
Always wear eye and hearing protection when loading and firing a firearm.
Some firearms will not open unless the safety is OFF.
The first vital rule (ACTS) is to assume every firearm is loaded.
Always point the firearm in the safest direction and never at yourself or anyone else.
Keep your finger off the trigger and out of the trigger guard except when firing.
Only hand over or accept a firearm that is open and unloaded.
PROVE stands for five steps: Point, Remove, Observe, Verify, Examine.
In PROVE, the Verify step means checking the feeding path for cartridges, cases or foreign objects.
In PROVE, Examine means checking the bore for lubricant, rust or obstructions.
A firearm proven safe stays safe only while the person who proved it keeps direct control (in sight and/or within reach).
Direct control means having the firearm in sight and/or within reach.
A muzzleloader is loaded with black powder or a substitute and fired by a percussion cap struck by the hammer.
A break (hinge) action opens near the breech and usually has one or two barrels.
A pump action is operated by sliding the fore-end back and forth and usually fires several shots.
A semi-automatic action extracts and ejects the empty case and chambers a new cartridge each time the trigger is pulled.
A lever action has a mechanical lever that opens the action and may fire one or several shots.
Mechanical safeties can fail, e.g., a sharp jolt may fire a firearm even with the safety ON; safe handling is the most important safety.
Safeties stop the firing sequence by blocking the trigger, sear, hammer or firing pin.
The sliding (tang) safety is usually on the right side of the receiver on rifles and on top of the receiver on shotguns.
A trigger block (lever) safety prevents a lever action from firing unless the lever is fully closed against the stock.
An exposed hammer has three positions; in the forward position it rests on the firing pin and a blow to it can fire the firearm.
On firearms designed for it, the half-cock position is considered safety ON and full cock is safety OFF.
A half-cock position is not necessarily a safety on every firearm; check the owner's manual and be careful as the hammer may slip under the thumb.
On a crossbolt safety, red usually means the safety is OFF and the firearm can fire, but there is no standard marking.
There is no standard marking for safety positions; if unmarked, unload and point safely before checking the owner's manual.
Before loading a firearm, identify the safety's ON position.
Do not handle a firearm unless you know how to operate it safely; otherwise get help from an instructor, the manual or a knowledgeable person.
When unloading a firearm with a detachable magazine, remove the magazine first, then open the action to clear the chamber.
Check the barrel for obstructions from the breech when possible; look from the muzzle only after confirming the firearm is unloaded, action open and chamber empty.
A cleaning patch that does not fully fill the bore may fail to reveal obstructions.
Load a firearm only when you intend to use it and only where it is legal and safe to do so.
When loading, match the firearm's stamp to the cartridge's, close the action, then put the safety ON if not already.
On a break action, the safety is usually on top of the action above the trigger, often a slide or an external hammer that must be fully forward or at half-cock.
To unload a break action, operate the release lever (the safety may need to be OFF) and 'break' the barrel open, removing shells by hand if not ejected.
A break action is usually closed by raising the stock sharply to lock the shells in the chambers.
A bolt action works like a door bolt; it is very strong and usually used on rifles; to unload, lift and pull the bolt handle back.
A bolt action works like a door bolt; it is very strong and usually used on rifles.
A repeating firearm has a single chamber but holds a supply of cartridges; the shooter must operate the action to chamber the next one (except semi-automatic).
The most common repeating actions are bolt, lever, pump and semi-automatic.
Reserve cartridges in repeating firearms are held in one of two types of magazine: box magazine or tubular magazine.
A tubular magazine can be located under the barrel or in the butt stock.
To unload a tubular magazine with a removable inner tube, remove the inner tube and let the cartridges fall out by gravity.
If a tubular magazine's inner tube is not removable, cycle the action several times, taking great care because the firearm is ready to fire.
Cartridges can stay stuck in a tubular magazine (dirt, rust, burr), so you must always see or touch the magazine follower to confirm it is empty.
Pointed centre-fire ammunition in a tubular magazine is dangerous because a bullet tip can detonate the primer of the cartridge ahead of it if the firearm is jarred.
Regulations limit semi-automatic centre-fire rifle and shotgun magazines to 5 cartridges.
The magazine capacity limits do not apply to rimfire rifles or to non-semi-automatic rifles (pump, lever, bolt).
Federal, provincial and territorial laws may set how many cartridges a magazine may hold while hunting; check with hunting authorities.
A bolt action works much like a door bolt; it is very strong and usually found on rifles.
On a bolt action, the safety is usually on the action above the trigger, left or right of the bolt, often a lever, or a slide directly behind the bolt.
Never rely on a safety: safeties wear out, and a firearm can discharge even with the safety engaged.
Before unloading any firearm, follow the vital four ACTS and PROVE it safe.
Only hand over or accept a firearm when it is open and unloaded.
First PROVE step: point the firearm in the safest direction throughout unloading, keep anything from touching the trigger, and apply the safety if it can stay on.
During unloading, engage the safety only if it can remain engaged while unloading.
To unload a bolt action, lift the bolt handle (usually up) and pull it back to extract and eject the cartridge; remove it by hand if it is not ejected.
If cartridges cannot be removed from the magazine any other way, cycle them all through the chamber to remove them.
PROVE includes verifying the feeding path is free of cartridges, cases or foreign objects, with the follower visible and touchable.
The last PROVE step is to examine the bore for lubricant, rust or obstructions every time you handle a firearm.
Direct control means having the firearm in sight and/or within reach.
A firearm proven safe stays safe only while the person who proved it keeps direct control of it.
Load a firearm only when you intend to use it and only where it is legal and safe to do so.
Before loading, choose ammunition whose markings match those on the barrel.
The first step in loading any firearm is to go through the full unloading procedure (ACTS and PROVE).
On a lever action, the safety is usually an external hammer with three positions; half-cock means the safety is ON.
With an external hammer fully forward resting on the firing pin, a sharp blow can discharge the firearm.
A lever action will not fire unless the lever is fully closed against the stock.
A lever action is opened by moving the lever down, which extracts and ejects any cartridge or case from the chamber.
A pump (slide) action is operated by moving the fore-end back and forth, allowing quick reloading without moving the muzzle off target; it is mostly used on shotguns.
On most pump actions, the safety is a slide or a button safety; button safeties are usually at the front or rear of the trigger guard, and the action release is near the trigger guard.
To unload a pump action, press the action release and pull the fore-end back to extract and eject the cartridge from the chamber.
A semi-automatic action uses part of the energy of expanding powder gases to extract the empty case and reload the chamber with each shot.
Some semi-automatics have an internal safety (disconnector) that prevents firing when the magazine is not in place; common external safeties are cross-bolt, slide and button.
When unloading a semi-automatic, remove the magazine first, then operate the cocking handle to extract the cartridge from the chamber.
Cartridges stuck in the chamber can be dangerous; consult a qualified person or gunsmith on how to clear the malfunction safely.
A good safety rule is not to put a cartridge in the chamber until you are ready to fire.
Range commands vary by sport, range and jurisdiction; learn your range's commands and ask the range officer if in doubt.
Shooters should wear safety glasses of impact-resistant glass or polycarbonate with side shields.
Target shooters risk eye injury from ejected cases, case fragments and other debris.
The noise of a gunshot is comparable to a nearby jet engine at take-off; unprotected exposure can cause hearing loss.
For the best hearing protection, wearing both earplugs and earmuffs is strongly recommended.
Disposable foam or wax earplugs can be used only once; reusable rubber plugs must be cleaned before and after each use.
If you fall while carrying a firearm, your first concern is to control the direction of the muzzle.
Button your collar and sleeves so a hot ejected case cannot get in and startle you into pointing the firearm dangerously or firing unintentionally.
At a certified range, the action must be open at all times except when ready to fire, and firearms are loaded, unloaded and fired only at the firing line.
At a range, no firearm may be loaded until the range officer gives the order.
On 'cease fire', stop firing immediately, unload, open the action, place the firearm on the mat or table pointed downrange, and step behind the cease-fire line.
During a cease-fire, no one may handle firearms or ammunition or return to the firing line until the range officer gives further orders.
In an emergency, anyone may call a cease-fire.
Minors and guests without a valid firearms licence must be under direct and immediate supervision when shooting, meaning the supervisor is within arm's length.
Unloaded firearms not in use are placed in designated racks with the action open or in a case; when moved, the muzzle points in the safest direction.
Shooters using semi-automatics should position themselves on the firing line where their ejected cases will not hit others.
Range etiquette: ask permission before handling another person's firearm or equipment, and do not smoke at the firing line.
Never leave a loaded firearm in or on a vehicle unless permitted to shoot from it; unload before getting in and load only after leaving the vehicle.
The term vehicle includes boats, cars, snowmobiles, sleds, private aircraft and ATVs; muzzle control is especially hard when getting in or out.
Do not shoot at game near the top of a hill, since people or livestock may be beyond it in the line of fire.
Water, rocks and flat surfaces can make a bullet ricochet or fragment.
When crossing a fence alone, unload, lay the firearm on the ground under the fence with the action open and the muzzle pointed away from where you cross.
When hunting alone from a pit or blind, unload the firearm and place it outside before entering, then retrieve it.
Use binoculars, never a rifle scope, to identify people, animals or objects.
For an informal firing line, the first step is to appoint a range officer who supervises all other steps.
In group shooting or hunting, everyone must agree on each person's zone of fire before starting and always know where partners are, since positions change.
The two-hand (ready) carry is the safest carry, giving the best control of the firearm and muzzle.
The shoulder carry is the least safe; it must not be used with a loaded firearm or around other people, and the muzzle must point up.
With the cradle carry, the muzzle points to one side, so a companion must walk on the side opposite the muzzle.
Do not use the elbow/side carry in brush (branches can turn the barrel toward you) or when people are in front; do not use the sling carry in thick brush.
Marksmanship is the ability to hit the target, and it is essential to safe shooting because you must know where the bullet will go.
Anticipation means foreseeing situations and evaluating the potential consequences of each shot before firing (ricochets, people beyond a hill, where the bullet goes if it passes through).
The four rifle shooting positions are standing, kneeling, sitting and prone; prone is the most stable.
The standing position is the least stable shooting position.
If you shake too much when standing, do not shoot; rest the rifle on a stable object such as a tree or rock, padding underneath.
When leaning against a tree or rock in the sitting position, make sure recoil will not push you against your support.
A shotgun is pointed rather than aimed: the shot spreads after leaving the barrel and covers a larger area than a single projectile.
With a moving target, keep following it (swinging) after firing a shotgun, otherwise the shot will hit behind the target.
With a shotgun, slap the trigger quickly but not too hard, whereas with a rifle you squeeze the trigger slowly and steadily.
With a rifle, squeeze the trigger slowly and progressively so that each shot comes as a surprise; jerking moves the firearm off target.

The four main types of sights are open (notch) sights, aperture (peep) sights, telescopic sights and electronic sights; most shotguns only have a bead front sight with the eye acting as the rear sight.
Sight alignment is lining up the rear sight and front sight on the target, which creates a sight picture; zeroing is done with the dominant eye.
Keep your eye back from a scope or sight to avoid injury to the eyebrow from recoil.
When shooting a shotgun, keep both eyes open, focus on the moving target (not the barrel or bead), and bring the stock to the cheek first, then the shoulder.
Fire during the natural respiratory pause after exhaling, rather than simply holding your breath.
Follow-through means maintaining the sight picture or shooting position after firing; otherwise the shot may miss.
An acceptable target is clearly identified, safe to shoot at and legal to shoot.
Before cleaning a firearm, you must apply the vital four ACTS and PROVE it safe (unloaded).
Repairs, even minor ones, should be done by qualified people; the average user should only do basic cleaning and lubrication.
The two main safety hazards that cleaning addresses are rust from moisture/condensation and excessive build-up of residue or rust, which can cause excess pressure and damage the barrel.
The barrel should be cleaned after every use; firearms using corrosive (old military) ammunition should be cleaned immediately after use.
A firearm stored for some time, or exposed to moisture or dust, must be thoroughly cleaned before use.
Excess oil or moisture is dangerous in cold weather: safeties or firing parts can freeze in the firing position and the gun may fire when it thaws.
When a firearm must be disassembled for cleaning, wear safety glasses and consult the owner's manual.
Whenever possible, clean the barrel from the breech toward the muzzle; if cleaning from the muzzle, keep the action open and avoid rubbing the rod against the muzzle.
Additional home precautions while cleaning: no ammunition nearby, never accept a loaded gun in a building, and give the task your full attention.
Cleaning method: after brushing with solvent, pass patches until one comes out clean, then a lightly oiled patch; before shooting again, run a dry patch to remove the oil.
Before using the firearm again, run a clean dry patch through the bore to remove oil or grease, because oil or dirt raises pressure and can burst the barrel.
Ammunition must be kept clean and dry, away from heat and vibration, and never cleaned with an oily cloth because penetrating oils harm primers.
After cleaning for storage, avoid touching metal parts with bare skin because acidic perspiration can cause rust.
Suicides and homicides are often impulsive acts, and many would not occur if firearms and ammunition were stored safely.
Making firearms and ammunition hard to access can delay impulsive acts long enough for the impulse to fade.
When a potentially violent situation is developing, remove all firearms even if properly stored, store them elsewhere and, if needed, inform police.
In case of a threat to public or personal safety, call local police immediately; for concerns, call the firearms line 1-800-731-4000 (chief firearms officer decides).
The chief firearms officer decides whether a person of concern may keep firearms.
Under the Criminal Code, owners must report lost or stolen firearms to local police and to the Canadian Firearms Program.
Reporting lost or stolen firearms is a legal obligation under the Criminal Code.
Owners are responsible for their firearms at all times; the law requires safe storage when you cannot exercise physical control, and unsafe storage is a criminal offence.
To deter theft, do not leave keys or combinations lying around, do not give them to others, and do not tell people you own firearms.
To prevent access by inexperienced or unauthorized users: disable the action (or use a trigger/cable lock), lock firearms out of sight, store ammunition separately, and supervise inexperienced users.
To avoid using the wrong ammunition, check it against the data stamped on the firearm and carry only ammunition suited to that firearm.
To prevent ricochets, take great care shooting at hard or flat surfaces or water, and check around and behind the target.
Ethical code: never use alcohol or drugs around firearms; even prescription or non-prescription medication (e.g., some allergy drugs) can impair reflexes, senses and balance.
Ethical code: always obtain permission before shooting on another's property (Crown, club or private land), and avoid shooting near buildings or roads.
Ethical code: explain firearm safety rules to all household members and keep keys or combinations out of reach of children and unauthorized adults.
Firearms commonly used for hunting or sport (rifles and shotguns) are generally non-restricted, though some rifles and shotguns are restricted or prohibited.
Some rifles and shotguns are restricted or prohibited; anyone wishing to acquire one should contact a chief firearms officer.
Individuals cannot acquire prohibited ammunition, such as tracer bullets that can start fires.
Prohibited devices that individuals cannot acquire include silencers and large-capacity magazines (except for rimfire cartridges).
Ammunition is defined as cartridges containing a projectile designed to be fired from a firearm, including caseless cartridges and shotgun shells.
By law, all firearms must be unloaded except when being used.

Storage of a non-restricted firearm: unloaded and either disabled by a secure locking device, or with bolt/bolt-carrier removed, or in a securely locked container, receptacle or room that cannot readily be broken into.
When storing a non-restricted firearm, ammunition must not be readily accessible unless it is stored in a securely locked container that cannot readily be broken into.
Storing ammunition in an unvented container can create an explosion hazard in case of fire.
Where shooting is legal, a non-restricted firearm used for predator control may be temporarily stored unlocked and in view if unloaded and ammunition is not readily accessible.
In a remote area where hunting may be necessary, a non-restricted firearm may be stored unlocked and in view with ammunition readily accessible, as long as the firearm is not loaded.
Display of a non-restricted firearm: unloaded; secured by a locking device or in a securely locked container/room; and not displayed with or near ammunition it can fire.
A non-restricted firearm must be unloaded during transport; exception: a muzzleloader may be carried loaded between hunting sites if the percussion cap or flint is removed.
A non-restricted firearm may be left in an unattended vehicle if unloaded and in a locked trunk or similar compartment.
If the unattended vehicle has no trunk, the unloaded firearm must be out of sight and the vehicle (or the part containing the firearm) locked.

In a remote area, a non-restricted firearm may be left in an unattended vehicle without a trunk (e.g., canoe, snowmobile) if out of sight, unloaded and fitted with a secure locking device unless needed for predator control.
To transport firearms on an airplane, contact the airline first for its rules and requirements.

Contravening the storage, display, transport and handling regulations is an indictable offence (max 2 years first offence, 5 years subsequent) or a summary offence; firearms and licence can also be taken away.
You may load a firearm or handle a loaded firearm only where it is legal to shoot; plan transport and home storage before buying, and transport firearms in an opaque or lockable case.
Pointing a firearm, loaded or not, at another person without lawful excuse is a criminal offence (max 5 years if indictable).
Buying ammunition in Canada requires a valid firearms licence (non-residents need a confirmed declaration or temporary borrowing licence).
Legally, a firearm includes its frame or receiver and anything that can be adapted for use as a firearm.
A non-restricted firearm is one that is neither prohibited nor restricted.
Restricted firearms include non-prohibited handguns, semi-automatic centrefire firearms with barrels under 470 mm, and firearms that can fire when folded or shortened below 660 mm.
Fully automatic firearms are prohibited, even if converted to fire one shot per trigger pull.
An antique firearm is one made before 1898 that was not designed or modified to use rimfire or centrefire ammunition.
A firearm is legally unloaded when no propellant, projectile or cartridge it can fire is in the breech, chamber or attached magazine.
A device designed to muffle or stop the sound of a firearm (silencer) and replica firearms are prohibited devices.
A secure locking device can only be opened with a key or combination and, once attached, prevents the firearm from being fired.
Anyone who wants to possess, borrow, buy, inherit or otherwise acquire a firearm must hold a valid firearms licence.
The possession-only licence (POL) is no longer issued to new applicants; it can be renewed as long as the holder still lawfully owns a firearm of that class.
A PAL is required to acquire any firearm, and applicants must first pass the relevant safety course or exams.
New PAL applicants face a waiting period of at least 28 days unless they already hold a POL, PAL or minor's licence.
The criteria for obtaining a firearms licence are the same across Canada.
Before transferring a firearm, the transferor must be reasonably sure the buyer has no mental illness threatening public safety, is not impaired, and must see a licence covering that class.
For a non-restricted transfer, the transferor must confirm the buyer holds a valid PAL with the proper privileges before completing it.
A restricted firearm transfer requires the Chief Firearms Officer's authorization, who issues a single transfer number to both parties.
